newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Japanese diplomat sees prosperity for HK.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japanese diplomat sees prosperity for HK.

text.p: Japan's envoy to Hong Kong is confident the territory will remain prosperous in the first years after its handover to China, but said its long-term success depends on continued autonomy.
That optimistic outlook was echoed by Japanese business leaders in the colony, who expect Hong Kong to remain a major Japanese trading partner long after the British yield control.
"Basically, we are confident in the future of Hong Kong," said Hideaki Ueda, consul-general of Japan, in an interview with Reuters.
He said he expected Hong Kong's free markets, regarded as the cornerstone of its prosperity, to remain unfettered after the transition.
Stressing that economic predictions were always difficult, Ueda nonetheless said he expected Hong Kong to enjoy economic prosperity over the next "two, three or four" years.
Beyond that, he said its success depended on Hong Kong maintaining its autonomy in the spirit of the "one country, two systems" promised by Beijing.

Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30. Beijing has promised Hong Kong's people will run the new Special Administrative Region, which will continue to enjoy its longstanding freedoms and capitalist way of life.

Japanese businesses will be watching to see whether Hong Kong's business atmosphere remains free-wheeling and the playing field level, local officials stay uncorrupt and government decisions are made by Hong Kong people, Ueda said.
"If they can succeed in establishing, practically, this autonomous power, then they will enjoy continuous prosperity."
Japanese business leaders were similarly optimistic.
"Generally speaking we are on the bullish side in the coming five years," said Yoshiaki Ishii, president of the Hong Kong Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
Ishii said he based his prediction on forecasts for China's economy, to which Hong Kong's economic fate is tied.

Japan has plenty at stake. Its non-financial direct investment in Hong Kong in 1995 totalled $1.14 billion, up slightly from 1993's $1.13 billion, according to statistics from the government-funded Hong Kong Trade Development Council (TDC).
Between 1989 and 1995, Japanese investment totalled $8.85 billion.
About 2,000 Japanese companies operate in Hong Kong. Ueda said about 22,000 Japanese nationals live in the colony.

Many Japanese companies use Hong Kong as a base for regional headquarters, controlling factories in southern China from Hong Kong's less restrictive regulatory environment, said Ishii. He estimated about 50 percent of the business done by Hong Kong-based Japanese companies was China-related.

Japanese companies are also active in Hong Kong's construction industry and its retailers operate five major department stores in the territory. In mid-1996, there were 48 Japanese banks, the largest group of foreign banks in the territory, TDC figures show.
The relationship is two-way. Japan is Hong Kong's third-largest export market, taking up to seven percent of its total exports, the TDC said.
Japanese tourists make up the second-largest group of visitors to Hong Kong in terms of spending. In 1995, they shelled out HK$14.1 billion, up 15.6 percent from 1994.
One of the few clouds in the partnership centres on an uninhabited rocky outcropping in the East China Sea claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan.
Late last year, nationalist fervour over the islands, called the Senkaku in Japanese and Diaoyu in Chinese, erupted when Japanese rightists landed and built a lighthouse.
The intensity of anti-Japanese sentiment and protests in Hong Kong surprised the territory's Japanese community, said Michael Martin, assistant chief economist at the TDC.
But the issue has since faded, said Martin, overshadowed by one that is more likely to slow the pace of Japanese investment in the colony -- the yen's devaluation over the past 18 months.
"If you sat down with a member of the Japanese business community today, the question that will jump to the fore will be the depreciation of the yen," Martin said.
The yen has been hardest hit by the strength of the U.S. dollar, which gained more than 50 percent against the yen since its all-time low of 79.75 yen in April 1995.
For some Japanese companies, it is no longer cheaper to manufacture abroad and then import the goods home, Martin said. Japanese companies are also becoming tighter with overseas investment, he said.

Ishii said a yen-driven exodus by Japanese companies was unlikely. "Once they set up a production line in Guangzhou, it's not easy for them to evacuate from there back to Japan if the yen has depreciated."
